newsitem.title: USA: Rubin - Dollar policy unchanged,but concerned on yen.
newsitem.headline: Rubin - Dollar policy unchanged,but concerned on yen.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Friday that U.S. dollar policy remains unchanged ahead of a weekend meeting of the Group of Seven.
Briefing reporters on the Sunday G7 meeting, Rubin said that he shared Japan's concern about the weakness of the yen, but added that he did not think that currencies should be used as trade tools.
"I expect we'll discuss exchange markets, as we always do," Rubin said, referring to the G7 meeting. "But I have nothing to add to my recent statements."
The G7 comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

Rubin has been criticized for his strong dollar policy by U.S. auto makers and other exporters who have complained that it has put them at a disadvantage in world markets, especially against their rivals from Japan.

Responding to that criticism, Rubin said that the U.S. focus should be on improving its own competitiveness through both private sector and government actions and not through attempted manipulation of exchange rates.
Rubin noted that the U.S. "clearly" has had a strong dollar. But at the same time, the economy has grown strongly for some time.

He played down concerns that the recent steep rise in long-term interest rates would hurt the U.S. economy and saw continued, solid growth and low inflation for the United States for the next year at least.
The United States also needs to work on promoting growth in the economies of its trading partners so as to increase demand for U.S. exports and to bring down its trade deficit, Rubin said.
"We do need to focus on the kinds of policies that other countries are pursuing," he said.

He said that Japan faces the challenge of maintaining a strong, domestic demand-led recovery and avoiding a significant rise in its trade surplus. That will be an "important focus" at the G7 meeting, he added.
He declined to make any specific policy prescriptions for Japan, though he did note the importance of deregulation in opening up Japan's economy.

Rubin said that the U.S. focus in Europe would also be on growth. Europe's plans to forge a monetary union might come up at the meeting, but Rubin said he did not expect that project to have a significant effect on the United States.
